headline: Tim Hortons App Briefly Becomes Most Effective Spy Agency in North America
subheadline: *Researchers found the coffee chain's loyalty app began transmitting data to a firm linked to Israeli military intelligence the moment it opened — roughly three seconds before users chose a cruller.*
author: Dale Prescott, Breakfast Intelligence Desk
seoTitle: Tim Hortons App Sent Data to Israeli Military-Linked Firm

altHeadlines: Millions of Canadians Shocked to Learn Donut Loyalty App Was Loyal to Someone Else
Your Double-Double Order Now Classified at 'Frosted' Clearance Level

body:
TORONTO — A beloved national institution was revealed this week to have quietly operated one of the most successful intelligence-gathering programmes in North American history, after researchers found that the Tim Hortons app began transmitting user data to an outside firm the moment it was opened — roughly three seconds before most users had even decided on a cruller.

The recipient, Forter, is a fraud-prevention company founded by veterans of Israeli military intelligence, which means every double-double purchased via the app was, technically, an act of international espionage with a loyalty points programme attached.

'The data starts flowing before you've scrolled the menu,' said one cybersecurity researcher. 'Somewhere, a server farm received a complete dossier on a man in Medicine Hat whose entire profile reads: will drive 40 minutes for a steeped tea, distrusts oat milk, once bought a Boston cream out of politeness.'

Privacy advocates said the harvested information was so granular it could determine whether a customer says 'Timbits' or 'donut holes,' a fault line intelligence analysts have reportedly been attempting to exploit for decades without success.

A Tim Hortons spokesperson stressed that the company takes loyalty extremely seriously. 'Both kinds,' the spokesperson clarified. 'Your loyalty to us, and our loyalty to whoever is asking. We are loyal to everyone, sequentially.'

Reaction among Canada's estimated five million accidental operatives was mixed. 'Honestly, I'm flattered,' said local man Graham Pelletier, 52, whose order history was described by one analyst as 'the most comprehensive file ever compiled on a person this boring.' 'CSIS — the actual spy agency — never wanted my data. Wouldn't even add me on Facebook.'

Experts noted the arrangement solved a problem that had bedevilled intelligence agencies for generations: how to convince millions of civilians to voluntarily install tracking software on their own phones. 'They tried everything,' said one former analyst. 'Turns out you just offer a free donut on their birthday.'

Documents reviewed by The Daily Absurd suggest the app's reward tiers were internally classified as 'asset,' 'super-asset,' and 'guy who has ordered the same thing every day for nine years and would absolutely notice if something was wrong.' The chain's popular Roll Up the Rim promotion has not been definitively linked to dead-drop tradecraft, though several winners reported finding 'report for debriefing' printed beneath their rims instead of a free coffee.

Rival chains confirmed they also share user data, though primarily with 'a guy named Darren,' who uses it mostly to judge people.

At press time, the app had transmitted this reporter's location, battery level and remaining dignity to three separate servers — and awarded him ten loyalty points for his cooperation.
